- When sentiment is high (≥ 0.6) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak predictions to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is low (≤ 0.4) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — model should not underestimate rebound potential.  
- After a recent spike in price, forecast should not overshoot the immediate prior peak; cap upward momentum at 10–15% below the peak.  
- If sentiment is trending upward (e.g., 0.5–0.75) and price is near a recent low, model should not underestimate the mean-reversion upward bias.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days show strong upward momentum, forecast should not be overly conservative — allow for 5–10% upward adjustment from recent mean.  
- If sentiment is flat or negative (≤ 0.3) and price is near a recent high, model should not over-predict continuation — expect mean reversion within 1–2 weeks.  
- When sentiment is volatile (e.g., alternating 0.3–0.7), avoid averaging — prioritize recent sentiment direction over historical trends.  
- If forecast is consistently 5–10% above true outcome over 3–5 days, reduce forecast by 2–3% per day to correct for overconfidence bias.
